books.section: The Rise of the Service Sector

stem: The trend in the chart most directly contributed to which of the following?

options.text: Slower wage growth for workers without a college degree
A sharp rise in the federal minimum wage
options.misconception: The minimum wage rose only in occasional small steps; a shrinking union movement did not push it up.

options.text: The return of child labor in American factories
options.misconception: Child labor laws stayed in place; no such return happened.

options.text: A national ban on strikes by public-sector workers
options.misconception: No national ban on public-sector strikes exists; the 1981 PATCO firing hit federal air-traffic controllers only.

rationales.A: Background: economists link weaker unions to weaker bargaining power, and Princeton notes wage stagnation followed the union decline.
rationales.B: The minimum wage is set by Congress, and it rose only in occasional small steps during these decades.
rationales.C: Child labor stayed illegal. Background: the chart is about adult union membership, not child labor.
rationales.D: Background: the PATCO firing of 1981 hit one federal union; it did not ban strikes nationwide.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what unions do for a worker: bargain together for pay, instead of each worker asking alone.
2. Background: as membership halved, that shared bargaining power thinned out with it.
3. Princeton ties the union decline to wage stagnation in the same decades.
4. The workers hit hardest were those with the least schooling, who had the fewest other options.
Remember: a union is a megaphone — halve the members, and the voice gets quieter.

| Year | Union members as a share of U.S. workers |

| 2000 | 13.4% |
| 2010 | 11.9% |

Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Population Survey. The 1979 figure comes from the pre-1983 historical series; 1983 onward is the comparable series.
